subStrands.citation: Grade 10 Computer Science Curriculum Design — Strand: Foundations of Computer Science — Sub-strand: Data Representation (illustrative; verify against official KICD PDF)
learningOutcomes: Explain how a computer represents numbers, text and images using binary digits
Convert whole numbers between binary, decimal and hexadecimal
Describe why computers use binary rather than decimal internally
boardNotes: Binary = base 2. Only two digits exist: 0 and 1.
Each binary digit is called a bit. 8 bits = 1 byte.
Computers use binary because circuits have two reliable states: on (1) and off (0).

activity.description: In pairs, learners convert their own age and their house number from decimal to binary by repeated division by 2, then swap books and check each other's working.
activity.materialsNeeded: None — exercise books and pens only.

assessmentQuestions.question: What are the only two digits used in binary?
Convert decimal 10 to binary.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 1010; 1 mark for correct working with a wrong final digit.

assessmentQuestions.question: How many bits make one byte?
Why do computers use binary instead of decimal?
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for referencing two reliable electrical states (on/off); 1 mark for a vaguer 'it's simpler for circuits' answer.

assessmentQuestions.question: Convert binary 1100 to decimal.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for 12; 1 mark for correct place-value setup (8+4+0+0) with an arithmetic slip.

subStrands.explainer: Binary is just counting using only two symbols instead of ten. Decimal place values go ...100,10,1; binary place values go ...8,4,2,1 — each one double the last. To convert decimal to binary, repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders bottom-to-top.

subStrands.citation: Grade 10 Computer Science Curriculum Design — Strand: Foundations of Computer Science — Sub-strand: Computer Hardware and Components (illustrative; verify against official KICD PDF)
learningOutcomes: Identify the main hardware components of a computer (CPU, RAM, storage, input/output devices)
Explain the role of the CPU and RAM in processing tasks
Distinguish between primary and secondary storage
boardNotes: CPU = 'brain' of the computer, executes instructions
RAM = short-term memory, cleared when power is off (volatile)
Storage (HDD/SSD) = long-term memory, keeps data when power is off (non-volatile)
Input devices (keyboard, mouse) -> Processing (CPU+RAM) -> Output devices (screen, speaker)

activity.description: Learners label a hand-drawn diagram of a computer's components on paper or on the board, then explain out loud the journey of a single keystroke from keyboard to screen.
activity.materialsNeeded: None — paper/board and pens only; no real computer required.

assessmentQuestions.question: Name one input device and one output device.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 1 mark each for a correct example (e.g. keyboard; screen).

assessmentQuestions.question: What does CPU stand for and what is its role?
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 1 mark for Central Processing Unit; 1 mark for 'executes instructions / does the processing'.

assessmentQuestions.question: What happens to the data in RAM when the computer is switched off?
Give one example of secondary storage.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 1 mark for a correct example (e.g. hard disk, SSD, flash drive).

assessmentQuestions.question: Explain briefly why a computer needs both RAM and storage instead of just one.
assessmentQuestions.markingScheme: 2 marks for contrasting speed/volatility of RAM with permanence of storage; 1 mark for a partial answer.

subStrands.explainer: Think of a computer like a kitchen: the CPU is the cook (does the work), RAM is the counter space (holds what you're using right now), and storage is the pantry (keeps things even when the kitchen is closed).
